```{r}
    height <- ave(x, x, FUN = seq_along)
    points(x, base[g] + 0.09 * height, pch = 16, cex = 0.8, col = grey)
    own <- sd(x) / sqrt(length(x)); pooled <- pooled_sd / sqrt(length(x))
    segments(mean(x) - c(own, pooled), base[g] - c(0.18, 0.42),
             mean(x) + c(own, pooled), base[g] - c(0.18, 0.42),
             col = c(blue, red), lwd = 4)
    points(rep(mean(x), 2), base[g] - c(0.18, 0.42), pch = 23, bg = gold,
           col = ink, cex = 1.1)
  }
  legend("bottomright", c("mean +/- 1 SE from the group's own SD",
                          "mean +/- 1 SE from the pooled SD"),
         col = c(blue, red), lwd = 4, bty = "n", cex = 0.75)
})
```

Pooling lends the usual group's tighter spread to the intensive group's
mean: the SE of that mean shrinks from its own 2.5298 points to 1.5811,
while the usual group's grows only from 0.6325 to 0.7906. The pooled SE
of the difference therefore understates the uncertainty that the ten
widely spread intensive scores carry.

[]{#ch03-justify-welch}

The justification of the equal-variance test in
[Section 5.3](#ch03-justify-equal-variance) carries over with three
changes: the target is a difference between two populations' means,
because the programmes were sampled rather than assigned; no common
spread is assumed, so the model assumptions concern each group mean,
above all the ten intensive scores, whose dot plot shows no single
dominating score; and Welch's variance model was chosen before the
scores were seen. Its bound is correspondingly modest: the interval
$[-0.7986,\ 10.7986]$, $p=.0837$, does not establish which programme
has the higher population mean.

How much does the variance model matter? @tbl-ch03-welch-simulation
answers by simulation. Each row generates 50,000 studies of two
independent samples from Normal populations with equal means and the
stated SDs, so every rejection of a zero difference rejects a true
null, and records how often each procedure's two-sided test at level
.05 rejects.

\Needspace{8\baselineskip}

| Group sizes | Population SDs | Equal-variance t | Welch's t |
|:--|:--|--:|--:|
| 10 and 40 | 8 and 4, as in the two-programme comparison | .1848 | .0507 |
| 10 and 40 | 4 and 8 | .0055 | .0513 |
| 25 and 25 | 8 and 4 | .0514 | .0493 |

: Rejection rates of a true zero difference at nominal level .05, from 50,000 simulated studies per design. {#tbl-ch03-welch-simulation tbl-colwidths="[16,48,18,18]"}

When the smaller group is the more variable, the equal-variance test
rejects the true null in .1848 of the studies instead of .05, so only
81.52% of its nominal 95% intervals cover the true difference; when the
smaller group is the less variable it rejects in only .0055, a test
that has become needlessly conservative and lost power. With equal
group sizes both tests stay near .05, and Welch's test stays near .05
in all three designs. This is why many texts recommend Welch's test
whenever the spreads may differ, and statistical software such as R
uses it by default [@delacre2017].

For Special Practice the two procedures nearly coincide: with 60
students in each group both SEs are 1.1325 points, so both give
$t=2.7372$, and Welch's df, 117.5119, fall just below 118 because the
SDs 6.0 and 6.4 are close but not equal, so both p-values display as
.0072. The agreement follows from equal group sizes and similar SDs; it
does not by itself establish equal population variances.

Choose between the procedures before the analysis, from the design and
subject knowledge: whether a common spread is plausible given how the
groups were formed and what the conditions might do to individual
responses, and whether the group sizes are equal. A preliminary test of
equal variances is not a good basis for the choice: the two-stage
procedure alters the error rates it is meant to protect, such tests
have least power in the small samples where the choice matters most,
and a nonsignificant variance test does not establish equal variances
[@zimmerman2004; @delacre2017]. Choosing whichever procedure excludes
zero is selecting an analysis after inspection, a problem Section 7.3
takes up.

## Association Between Categorical Variables: The Chi-Square Test {#sec-categorical-comparison}

The test logic of Section 4 is not limited to means. Chapter 2,
Section 3.1, described the relationship between two categorical
variables with conditional proportions, comparing passing among
students with and without a higher-education intention. Such a
relationship is an **association** between categorical variables: the
distribution of one variable changes across the categories of the
other. When the outcome is a category, such as completed or not, each
record falls in one cell of a table and the data are counts. This
section builds a test of association with the same three parts as the
tests of Section 4: a null hypothesis, a statistic that measures
departure from it, and a reference distribution for that statistic.
Its last subsection reads tables of three or more categorical
variables.

### Counts, proportions and expected counts

Consider an invented teaching model with 100 independently sampled
learners. For each learner the participation format, Online or In
person, and whether the learner completed the course were recorded. The
format was observed rather than randomly assigned, so the question
concerns association: is completion related to format?
@tbl-ch03-two-way crosses the two variables in a **two-way table**,
with one cell for each combination and the totals in the margins. The
number of ways counts the variables crossed, not their categories: a
table of three formats by completion would still be a two-way table.

\Needspace{8\baselineskip}

| Participation format | Completed | Did not complete | Total | Completion proportion |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Online | 32 | 18 | 50 | .64 |
| In person | 18 | 32 | 50 | .36 |
| Total | 50 | 50 | 100 | .50 |

: Invented counts of completion by participation format for 100 learners. {#tbl-ch03-two-way tbl-colwidths="[28,16,20,12,24]"}

Among the 50 Online learners 32 completed, a **conditional proportion**
of $32/50=.64$; among the 50 In-person learners 18 completed,
$18/50=.36$. Each proportion divides by its own format's total, so
the two formats can be compared even when their sizes differ. The
Online-minus-In-person difference is .28, or 28 percentage
points. @fig-ch03-completion draws the two proportions beside the
.5 of all 100 learners.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ch03-completion
#| fig-cap: "Completion by participation format in the invented table of 100 learners. Each bar divides one format's 50 learners into those who completed (dark) and those who did not (light); the dashed line marks the completion proportion of all 100 learners, .5, which both formats would share if format and completion were independent."
#| fig-alt: "Two horizontal bars, Online above In person, each running from 0 to 1. The dark completed part reaches .64 for Online and .36 for In person, with the remainders .36 and .64 in a light shade. A dashed red line at .5 is labelled as the proportion of all 100 learners; the Online bar's completed part extends past it and the In-person bar's stops short of it."
#| fig-width: 7.2
#| fig-height: 1.9
#| fig-pos: "!ht"

local({
  completed <- c("In person" = 18 / 50, Online = 32 / 50)
  p2 <- function(p) fmt4(p, lead = FALSE)
  saved_par <- par(mar = c(3.6, 6.2, 1.2, 1.0), mgp = c(2.2, 0.6, 0))
  on.exit(par(saved_par))
  at <- barplot(rbind(completed, 1 - completed), horiz = TRUE,
                col = c(blue, blue_light), border = ink, xlim = c(0, 1),
                las = 1, xlab = "Proportion of the format's 50 learners",
                space = 0.5, col.axis = ink, col.lab = ink, axes = FALSE)
  axis(1, at = seq(0, 1, .25), labels = c("0", ".25", ".50", ".75", "1"),
       col.axis = ink)
  text(completed / 2, at, paste("completed", p2(completed)),
       col = "white", cex = 0.83)
  text((1 + completed) / 2, at, paste("did not", p2(1 - completed)),
       col = ink, cex = 0.83)
  abline(v = .5, lty = 2, col = red, lwd = 1.4)
  text(.5, max(at) + 0.75, "all 100 learners: .5", pos = 4,
       offset = 0.3, cex = 0.83, col = red, xpd = TRUE)
})
```

\Needspace{8\baselineskip}

Are the two rates different enough, beyond sampling variation, to
indicate an association in the population? The test sets two
hypotheses about the stipulated population or process:

$$
\begin{aligned}
H_0&:\ \text{format and completion are not associated},\\
H_A&:\ \text{format and completion are associated}.
\end{aligned}
$$

No association means that format and completion are **independent**:
the completion probability is the same in both formats. Estimated from
all the records, that common probability is
$50/100=.5$, so independence predicts 25 completions among the 50
Online learners and 25 among the 50 In-person learners. In general a
cell's **expected count** is

$$
E_{rc}=\frac{(\text{row }r\text{ total})(\text{column }c\text{ total})}{n},
$$

which for the Online/Completed cell gives $50\times50/100=25$. Expected
counts keep the observed margins while imposing the null relationship,
and in other tables they need not be whole numbers.
@tbl-ch03-counts sets the observed counts beside the expected ones.

\Needspace{8\baselineskip}

| Participation format | Observed: completed | Observed: did not | Expected: completed | Expected: did not |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Online | 32 | 18 | 25 | 25 |
| In person | 18 | 32 | 25 | 25 |
| Total | 50 | 50 | 50 | 50 |

: Observed counts and the counts expected under independence, with the same margins. {#tbl-ch03-counts tbl-colwidths="[24,19,19,19,19]"}

Every observed count lies 7 from its expected count: more Online and
fewer In-person learners completed than independence predicts.

### The chi-square statistic and its distribution

Pearson's **chi-square statistic** gathers the departures into one
number. Each observed-minus-expected difference is squared, so that
departures in either direction count, and divided by its expected
count, so that a departure is judged against the size of its cell:

$$
X^2=\sum_{\text{cells}}\frac{(O_{rc}-E_{rc})^2}{E_{rc}}.
$$

Here each of the four cells contributes $(32-25)^2/25=1.96$, so
$X^2=7.84$. A table that matched independence exactly would give 0,
and larger values mean larger departures.

How large is large? If format and completion are independent, $X^2$
follows approximately a **chi-square distribution**. Panel (a) of
@fig-ch03-chisq shows that this is a family of right-skewed
distributions on positive values whose shape is set by the degrees of
freedom: the mean of each curve equals its df, so the curves move right
and spread out as the df grow. For a two-way table with $r$ rows and
$c$ columns the df are $(r-1)(c-1)$. In a two-by-two table, once the
row and column totals are fixed, the count in one cell determines the
other three, so only one cell is free to depart from independence and
$df=(2-1)(2-1)=1$.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ch03-chisq
#| fig-cap: "The chi-square reference. (a) Chi-square distributions with 1, 4 and 8 degrees of freedom: right-skewed curves on positive values whose centre and spread grow with the df. (b) The upper tail of the distribution with 1 df, the reference for a two-by-two table, enlarged on its own vertical scale: the shaded area beyond the .05 critical value 3.8415 holds .05, and the dark part beyond the observed statistic 7.84 is the p-value, $p=.0051$."
#| fig-alt: "Two panels. The first shows three density curves on an axis from 0 to 20: with 1 degree of freedom the curve falls steeply from a high value near zero; with 4 it peaks near 2; with 8 it peaks near 6 and spreads further right. The second enlarges the upper tail of the curve with 1 degree of freedom, from 3 to 12 on a density axis up to 0.04: a dashed grey line at 3.8415 is labelled critical 3.8415, .05 beyond, and the region beyond it is shaded light red; a red mark at 7.84 is labelled observed 7.84, p = .0051 beyond, and the smaller region beyond it is dark red."
#| fig-width: 7.2
#| fig-height: 2.9
#| fig-pos: "!ht"

local({
  saved_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.0, 3.6, 1.8, 0.6),
                   mgp = c(2.3, 0.6, 0))
  on.exit(par(saved_par))
  x <- seq(0.02, 20, length.out = 1000)
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 20), ylim = c(0, 0.5), yaxs = "i",
       xlab = "Value of the chi-square statistic", ylab = "Density",
       main = "(a) Chi-square distributions", cex.main = 0.85,
       font.main = 1, col.main = ink, col.axis = ink, col.lab = ink)
  dfs <- c(1, 4, 8); colours <- c(red, blue, gold)
  for (k in 1:3) lines(x, dchisq(x, dfs[k]), col = colours[k], lwd = 1.8)
  text(c(1.6, 3.4, 9.2), c(0.33, 0.2, 0.125), paste("df =", dfs),
       pos = 4, col = colours, cex = 0.83)
  critical <- qchisq(.95, 1); observed <- 7.84
  shade <- function(from, to, col) {
    g <- seq(from, to, length.out = 200)
    polygon(c(from, g, to), c(0, dchisq(g, 1), 0), col = col, border = NA)
  }
  x1 <- seq(3, 12, length.out = 600)
  plot(NA, xlim = c(3, 12), ylim = c(0, 0.04), yaxs = "i",
       xlab = "Value of the chi-square statistic", ylab = "Density",
       main = "(b) Upper tail of df = 1, enlarged", cex.main = 0.85,
       font.main = 1, col.main = ink, col.axis = ink, col.lab = ink)
  shade(critical, 12, "#F4C7C7"); shade(observed, 12, red)
  lines(x1, dchisq(x1, 1), col = ink, lwd = 1.8)
  segments(critical, 0, critical, 0.038, col = grey, lty = 2, lwd = 1.2)
  text(critical, 0.0368, paste0("critical ", fmt4(critical), ": .05 beyond"),
       pos = 4, offset = 0.15, col = grey, cex = 0.83)
  segments(observed, 0, observed, 0.016, col = red, lwd = 1.6)
  text(observed, 0.016, paste0("observed ", fmt4(observed), "\np = ",
       fmt4(pchisq(observed, 1, lower.tail = FALSE), lead = FALSE), " beyond"),
       pos = 4, offset = 0.15, col = red, cex = 0.83)
})
```

Only the upper tail counts. Because every contribution is squared,
departures from independence in either direction make $X^2$ larger, so
the p-value is the area beyond the observed statistic in the upper
tail. Panel (b) enlarges the upper tail of the chi-square distribution
with 1 df: 5% of it lies beyond the critical value 3.8415, and the
observed 7.84 lies well beyond that, cutting off the dark upper-tail
area $p=.0051$. If format and completion were
independent, a table departing from independence at least this much
would arise in about 5 of every 1,000 samples of 100 learners.

### Reading the result and its conditions

Under the stipulated model, the table gives evidence against
independence. The proportions give the direction and size that the
squared statistic discards: completion is 28 percentage points
more frequent in the Online group. This observed association does not
establish that assigning a format would change completion, because
learners chose or were placed in their formats by processes the table
does not record.

\Needspace{6\baselineskip}

[]{#ch03-justify-counts}

::: {.callout-tip title="Justifying the analysis"}
- **Target:** Whether participation format and completion are associated
  in the stipulated population, with direction and size given by the
  completion proportions, .64 Online and .36 In person.
- **Conditions:**
  - *Secured by design:* 100 independently sampled learners, each
    counted once in exactly one of the four cells. The format was
    observed, not assigned.
  - *Model assumptions:* Expected counts large enough for the chi-square
    reference with 1 df to approximate the statistic's distribution
    under independence.
  - *Choices and defaults:* Pearson's statistic without a continuity
    correction, as calculated above; the upper tail, because only large
    discrepancies count against independence; level .05; Online minus
    In person for the proportion difference.
- **Check:** Every expected count is 25, far above the small counts at
  which the approximation weakens; a common guideline flags expected
  counts below 5, where an exact test (Chapter 6) would take its place.
  Independence of the records cannot be checked from the table: learners
  counted twice or sharing a class would make the counts overstate the
  information.
- **Bound:** Evidence against independence in the stipulated
  population, $X^2(1)=7.84$, $p=.0051$, with a completion proportion
  .28 higher Online. Because the format was observed rather than
  assigned, the table does not show that assigning a format would change
  completion.
:::

Statistical software often applies a continuity correction to a
two-by-two table by default, a related but different calculation;
Chapter 6 reproduces the uncorrected statistic taught here in R and
develops further categorical analyses. Exercise 7 supplies a separate
200-record table for applying the same reasoning.

### Three or more categorical variables {#sec-ch03-multiway}

A two-way table holds two categorical variables. Crossing a third gives
a **three-way table**, and a fourth a four-way table; any table of
three or more is a **multiway table**. Suppose the invented record had
also noted whether each learner had studied the subject before, with
25 learners of each format in each prior-study group.
@tbl-ch03-three-way arranges the same 100 learners by prior study,
format and completion. It is read as two-way tables within the
**layers** of the third variable: one format-by-completion table for
the learners who had studied the subject before, and one for those new
to it. Adding the two layers cell by cell returns the two-way table of
Section 6.1.

\Needspace{12\baselineskip}

| Prior study | Participation format | Completed | Did not complete | Total | Completion proportion |
|:--|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Studied before | Online | 19 | 6 | 25 | .76 |
|  | In person | 15 | 10 | 25 | .60 |
| New to the subject | Online | 13 | 12 | 25 | .52 |
|  | In person | 3 | 22 | 25 | .12 |
| Both layers added | Online | 32 | 18 | 50 | .64 |
|  | In person | 18 | 32 | 50 | .36 |

: Invented counts of completion by participation format within two layers of prior study, for the same 100 learners. {#tbl-ch03-three-way tbl-colwidths="[25,19,15,16,9,16]"}

Within each layer, Online learners completed more often: .76 against
.60 among those who had studied the subject before, a difference of
.16, and .52 against .12 among those new to it, a difference of .40.
Prior study also goes with completion in both formats. Because each
layer holds the same number of learners of each format, the added
table's difference, .28, lies midway between the layer differences.
When the layers hold different mixes of the groups compared, the added
table can differ from every layer; Chapter 14 reads a real admissions
table in which the added comparison points the other way from most of
its layers.

The chi-square test of Sections 6.1--6.3 applies to any one two-way
table in the display. Applied to one layer, it asks whether format and
completion are associated among that layer's 50 learners; applied to
the added table, it asks the question of Section 6.1, with prior study
set aside. No test of one two-way table answers a question about the
three variables jointly: whether the format difference is the same in
both layers, or whether format and completion are associated once
prior study is held fixed, with all 100 learners used at once. Such
questions need a method that uses all three variables at once, such as
the models for multiway tables that begin with logistic regression in
Chapter 11.

Comparing the two layers' tests does not settle whether their
associations differ. Each layer's p-value depends on the size of its
association and on the number of learners in the layer, so a p-value
below .05 in one layer beside one above .05 in the other shows that the
evidence differs, not that the associations do [@gelman2006]. The
difference between the layer differences, .40 against .16, is a
quantity with its own uncertainty, which a joint model estimates.

A fourth variable, such as the term in which a learner enrolled, adds a
second layer variable. The four-way table is read as two-way tables
within each combination of the two layer variables, four layers when
each has two categories, and every added variable divides the same
learners among more layers, leaving fewer records in each.

## Magnitude, Uncertainty, and Several Results {#sec-ch03-interpretation}

### Magnitude and practical importance

The special-practice estimate, interval, test, and benchmark answer
different parts of the substantive question. The raw difference is
3.1 points. Its approximate interval [0.8572, 5.3428] lies above zero and
agrees with the two-sided $p=.0072$ result. It also spans the
course-specific two-point importance criterion.

Consequently, a positive mean assignment effect is supported under
the procedure, while its practical importance remains unresolved.
Effects below the criterion and effects clearly above it are both
compatible with the data. The estimate exceeding two points does not
settle this issue. Nor would an interval crossing zero automatically
mean that all effects of practical interest had been ruled out.

A **standardized mean difference** expresses a raw difference relative
to a named SD. One familiar denominator is the pooled SD of Section 2.2,
$s_p=6.2032$ points, which gives

$$
d=\frac{\bar y_1-\bar y_0}{s_p}=\frac{3.1}{6.2032}=.4997.
$$

The mean difference is about half of this particular within-group SD.
Hedges' correction adjusts $d$ for small-sample bias under its
reference model; its usual approximation multiplies $d$ by a factor
just below one [@lakens2013]:

$$
g\approx d\left(1-\frac{3}{4(n_1+n_0)-9}\right)=.4966.
$$

Changing the denominator changes the comparison's scale. It does not
broaden the participant scope or supply a universal importance threshold.
For the current course decision, assessment points and the two-point
benchmark remain the most direct terms. Chapter 4 develops effect-size
interpretation across group comparisons.

### Errors, power, and precision planning

A test ends in a decision, to reject the null or not to reject it, and
the decision can be wrong in two ways. A **Type I error** rejects a
null hypothesis that is true. Its probability is the significance level
$\alpha$, chosen in advance: a level-.05 rule applied when the null and
the procedure's conditions hold rejects in 5% of repetitions. A **Type
II error** fails to reject a null that is false. Its probability,
$\beta$, depends on how far the truth lies from the null, so it is
defined only under a specified alternative, such as a true difference
of three points. The **power** of the test at that alternative is the
probability that it rejects there, $1-\beta$: the chance that the study
detects an effect of that size. @tbl-ch03-errors sets out the four
combinations of decision and truth; it says *do not reject* because
the decision does not reveal that the null is true.

\Needspace{9\baselineskip}

| Decision | Null is true | Specified alternative is true |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Do not reject $H_0$ | Correct nonrejection; probability $1-\alpha$ for an exactly calibrated continuous test | Type II error; probability $\beta$ at this alternative |
| Reject $H_0$ | Type I error; probability $\alpha$ for that calibrated test | Correct rejection; power $1-\beta$ at this alternative |

: Decisions and error probabilities under specified states of the model. {#tbl-ch03-errors tbl-colwidths="[22,39,39]"}

Both error probabilities condition on a state of the model; neither is
the probability that the decision in one completed study is wrong. For
an approximately calibrated procedure, nominal $\alpha$ need not equal
the actual rejection probability, as the Welch demonstration of Section
5.4 showed.

These probabilities matter most when a study is planned, and planning
can serve two purposes. **Precision planning** asks for an interval
narrow enough for the intended use. For a separate independent
two-group study, suppose each group has anticipated SD 6.2 points and
we want a 95% interval with half-width 2 points. With $n$ per group the
half-width is about $h=z^*\sigma\sqrt{2/n}$, and solving for $n$ gives

$$
n\approx2\left(\frac{z^*\sigma}{h}\right)^2
=2\left(\frac{1.96\times6.2}{2}\right)^2=73.8356,
$$

so 74 observed outcomes per group. The calculation uses a stipulated SD
and an independent-sampling approximation; it does not redesign the
fixed 120-participant study.

**Power planning** asks how likely the study is to reject a zero
difference when a specified difference is real. At 74 per group the SE
of the estimated difference is $6.2\sqrt{2/74}=1.0193$ points. Treating
the planning SD as known, so that the Normal reference applies, a
two-sided .05 test rejects when the estimate lies beyond $\pm1.9977$
points. Panel (a) of @fig-ch03-errors-power draws two sampling
distributions of the estimate on one axis, under the null, centred at
zero, and under an alternative with a true difference of 3 points,
together with that one rejection rule. The null's two outer tails hold
$\alpha/2=.025$ each: a rejection there is a Type I error. Under the
alternative, the hatched area between the boundaries, $\beta=.1627$, is
the probability of a Type II error, and the rest of its curve, .8373,
is the power at 3 points. Moving the alternative further from zero, or
narrowing both curves with a larger sample, shrinks $\beta$ and raises
the power.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ch03-errors-power
#| fig-cap: "Errors and power for a planned study with 74 per group, outcome SD 6.2 and a two-sided .05 test, adapted from @biau2010. (a) Sampling distributions of the estimated difference under the null (true difference 0) and under an alternative (true difference 3), with the rejection boundaries $\\pm1.9977$: the null's dark outer tails hold $\\alpha/2=.025$ each; under the alternative, the hatched area between the boundaries is $\\beta=.1627$ and the light area beyond them is the power, .8373. (b) Power of the same rule across true differences for 37, 74 and 148 per group."
#| fig-alt: "Two panels. The first shows two bell-shaped curves of equal height on an estimated-difference axis, a solid null curve centred at 0 and a dashed alternative curve centred at 3, with dashed boundary lines at minus and plus 1.9977 marked on the axis. The null curve's two small outer tails are dark blue; under the alternative curve the region between the boundaries is hatched red and labelled beta = .1627, and the larger region beyond 1.9977 is light blue and labelled power = .8373. The second plots power against true differences from 0 to 5 points for 37, 74 and 148 per group; every curve starts at .05, the 74-per-group curve passes .5009 at 2 and .8373 at 3, and the 148-per-group curve reaches .7925 at 2, just below a dotted line at .8."
#| fig-width: 7.2
#| fig-height: 3.1
#| fig-pos: "!ht"

local({
  plan_se <- 6.2 * sqrt(2 / 74)
  cutoff <- qnorm(.975) * plan_se
  power_at <- function(delta, n, sigma = 6.2) {
    se <- sigma * sqrt(2 / n); cut <- qnorm(.975) * se
    pnorm(-cut, delta, se) + 1 - pnorm(cut, delta, se)
  }
  saved_par <- par(mar = c(2.9, 2.9, 1.5, 0.4), mgp = c(1.75, 0.45, 0),
                   tcl = -0.3, cex.axis = 0.8, cex.lab = 0.84,
                   cex.main = 0.88, font.main = 1, col.main = ink,
                   col.axis = ink, col.lab = ink)
  on.exit(par(saved_par))
  layout(matrix(1:2, nrow = 1), widths = c(1.4, 1))
  x <- seq(-4.5, 7.5, length.out = 1201)
  null_d <- dnorm(x, 0, plan_se); alt_d <- dnorm(x, 3, plan_se)
  area <- function(keep, dens, ...) {
    polygon(c(x[keep], rev(x[keep])), c(dens[keep], rep(0, sum(keep))), ...)
  }
  plot(NA, xlim = c(-4.5, 7.5), ylim = c(0, 0.78), yaxs = "i", xaxt = "n",
       xlab = "Estimated difference (points)", ylab = "Density",
       main = "(a) One rejection rule, two possible truths")
  axis(1, at = c(-4, -cutoff, 0, cutoff, 4, 6),
       labels = c("-4", "-1.9977", "0", "1.9977", "4", "6"))
  area(x >= cutoff, alt_d, col = "#CFE3EC", border = NA)
  area(abs(x) < cutoff, alt_d, col = red, border = NA, density = 24,
       angle = 45)
  area(x <= -cutoff, null_d, col = blue, border = NA)
  area(x >= cutoff, null_d, col = blue, border = NA)
  lines(x, null_d, col = ink, lwd = 1.8)
  lines(x, alt_d, col = ink, lwd = 1.8, lty = 5)
  segments(c(-cutoff, cutoff), 0, c(-cutoff, cutoff), 0.3, col = grey,
           lty = 2, lwd = 1.2)
  curves <- legend("topleft", c("null: true difference 0",
                                "alternative: true difference 3"),
                   lty = c(1, 5), lwd = 1.8, col = ink, bty = "n",
                   cex = 0.83)
  legend(curves$rect$left, curves$rect$top - curves$rect$h + 0.03,
         legend = c(expression(paste(alpha, "/2 = .025 each tail")),
                    expression(paste(beta, " = .1627")), "power = .8373"),
         fill = c(blue, red, "#CFE3EC"), border = c(ink, red, ink),
         density = c(NA, 30, NA), angle = 45, bty = "n", cex = 0.83)
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 5), ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "True difference (points)",
       ylab = "Power", main = "(b) Power across true differences")
  abline(h = c(.05, .80), lty = 3, col = grey)
  difference <- seq(0, 5, length.out = 201)
  sizes <- c(37, 74, 148); colours <- c(grey, blue, red); types <- c(2, 1, 4)
  for (k in 1:3) lines(difference, power_at(difference, sizes[k]),
                       col = colours[k], lty = types[k], lwd = 2)
  marked <- c(power_at(c(2, 3), 74), power_at(2, 148))
  points(c(2, 3, 2), marked, pch = 21, bg = gold, col = ink, cex = 1.1)
  text(c(2, 3, 2), marked + c(0, 0, 0.08),
       fmt4(marked, lead = FALSE), pos = c(4, 4, 2), cex = 0.83)
  legend("bottomright", paste(sizes, "per group"), col = colours,
         lty = types, lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = 0.83, inset = c(0, 0.08))
})
```

Panel (b) repeats the calculation across true differences for three
group sizes. Every curve starts at .05 at a true difference of zero,
where a rejection is a Type I error, and rises with the true difference
and the group size; a smaller outcome SD would raise it too. At 74 per
group, the size chosen for a two-point half-width, power is .5009 at a
true difference of 2 points, about an even chance of rejecting at the
benchmark itself, and .8373 at 3 points; doubling to 148 per group
raises power at 2 points to .7925. Reaching power .8 at 2 points takes
about 151 per group (152 with the t reference), roughly twice the
number that precision planning gave. A study has a power curve, not one
power value, and a sample size chosen for precision is not
automatically a power target.

Planning also needs a plausible spread, allocation, dependence
structure, procedure, sidedness, threshold, measurement quality and
feasible follow-up. For a class-assigned study, additional randomly assigned classes supply information that more students
within existing classes cannot replace, as the design effect of Section
2.3 quantifies. If 10% of outcomes are expected to be unavailable
independently of relevant outcomes, recruiting at least 83 per group
($74/.9=82.2222$) gives 74 on average, which neither guarantees
complete data nor repairs bias from selective attrition.

[]{#app-ch03-thousand-studies}

Error probabilities describe a rule applied over many studies, not a
single result. Suppose, as stipulated expected counts rather than data,
that 900 of 1,000 studies test a true null and 100 test a specified
alternative, each at $\alpha=.05$ with power .8 at its alternative
(@tbl-ch03-thousand).

\Needspace{8\baselineskip}

| Model state | Reject | Do not reject | Total |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| True null | 45 | 855 | 900 |
| Specified alternative | 80 | 20 | 100 |
| Total | 125 | 875 | 1,000 |

: Expected decisions under stipulated prevalence, alpha and power. {#tbl-ch03-thousand tbl-colwidths="[40,20,20,20]"}

The Type I error probability is $45/900=.05$ and the Type II error
probability $20/100=.2$, but among the 125 expected rejections,
$45/125=.36$ come from true nulls. This false-positive fraction has a
different denominator: it changes with the share of true nulls and with
the power, and it is neither an observed p-value nor a probability for
one completed study.

### Choices made after seeing the results {#sec-ch03-selection}

One analysis can be part of a larger search. A researcher might inspect
several outcomes, subgroups, models, exclusion rules or stopping
points, then report the most favorable result. The reported tail area
can still be calculated, but a calibration for one advance-specified
test does not cover that selection process [@simmons2011]. A report
should therefore say which decisions were made before and which after
the relevant results were examined. Choosing in advance makes the
intended comparison and the scope for selection visible; a comparison
noticed later can still be informative when its exploratory origin is
reported with it.

Selection also changes what the retained estimates look like. Consider
a Normal sampling model with true difference 1 point and known SE 2
points. A two-sided .05 test of zero using the critical value 1.96
retains only estimates above 3.92 or below $-3.92$
(@fig-ch03-selection).

```{r}
#| label: fig-ch03-selection
#| fig-pos: "!ht"
#| fig-cap: "A significance filter retains both tails of a Normal estimate distribution centered at the true difference of one point, with known SE two points."
#| fig-alt: "Normal density centered at one, with a gold line at the true difference labelled above the peak and dashed red lines at minus and plus 3.92. The shaded tails beyond them are labelled: selected estimates below minus 3.92 have the wrong sign, and selected estimates above 3.92 substantially exceed the true effect."
#| fig-width: 6.8
#| fig-height: 2.3
local({
  saved_par <- par(mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 0.6, .7))
  on.exit(par(saved_par))
  x <- seq(-7, 9, length.out = 1601)
  plot(x, dnorm(x, 1, 2), type = "l", lwd = 2, col = ink, ylim = c(0, .235),
       xlab = "Estimated difference (points)", ylab = "Density")
  for (selected in list(x[x < -3.92], x[x > 3.92])) {
    polygon(c(selected, rev(selected)),
            c(dnorm(selected, 1, 2), rep(0, length(selected))),
            col = "#F4C7C7", border = NA)
  }
  lines(x, dnorm(x, 1, 2), lwd = 2, col = ink)
  abline(v = 1, col = gold, lwd = 2)
  abline(v = c(-3.92, 3.92), col = red, lty = 2)
  text(1, .222, "true difference = 1", pos = 2, offset = 0.3, cex = .8,
       col = gold)
  text(-3.92, .105, "-3.9200", pos = 2, cex = .8, col = red)
  text(3.92, .105, "3.9200", pos = 4, cex = .8, col = red)
  text(-5.6, .055, "selected:\nwrong sign", cex = .72, col = red)
  text(6.9, .065, "selected:\nexaggerated", cex = .72, col = red)
})
```

The selected positive estimates are much larger than the truth; the
selected negative estimates have the wrong sign. The underlying estimand
stays at one point, while selection changes which estimates are retained.
The estimator's original unbiasedness and its interval's unconditional
coverage need not hold within this selected set.

[]{#app-ch03-planning}

Running several tests raises a related problem. Each test at level .05
carries its own 5% chance of a false rejection, so five independent
tests of true nulls have probability $1-.95^5=.2262$ of at least one.
Chapter 4 develops how a declared family of comparisons controls that
chance.

\Needspace{16\baselineskip}

### Report the result with its conditions and scope

| Item | Result |
|:--|:--|
| Design and follow-up | 120 consenting students, 60 randomly assigned to each format; all 120 delayed scores observed |
| Mean difference, Special minus Usual | 3.1 points (27.1 versus 24.0) |
| Standard error of the difference | 1.1325 points |
| 95% confidence interval | [0.8572, 5.3428] points |
| Two-sided test from the same procedure | $t(118)=2.7372$, $p=.0072$ |
| Benchmark for potential importance | 2 points; fixed before outcome access, course-specific |

: The invented special-practice study and its results. {#tbl-ch03-study-record tbl-colwidths="[44,56]"}

The table assembles results already developed; the group summaries stay
in @tbl-ch03-observed. A useful results paragraph explains how they
relate, rather than substituting the phrase “Special Practice worked”
for the comparison:

> Among the 120 consenting first-year students randomly assigned to
> Special Practice or Usual Practice, the mean delayed-assessment
> score was 3.1 points higher under Special Practice (27.1 versus
> 24.0 on the 0--40 assessment), with an approximate 95% interval
> from 0.8572 to 5.3428 points and $p=.0072$ for the two-sided test of
> no difference. The comparison and the two-point benchmark for
> practical importance were chosen before the outcomes were seen. The
> interval excludes zero but spans the benchmark, so the direction is
> well supported while the practical importance of the difference
> remains unresolved. The result concerns these participants, this
> assessment two weeks after four sessions, and the equal-variance
> working procedure; it does not by itself speak to attendance,
> mechanisms, durable learning, or students elsewhere.

Random assignment supports the participant comparison, and complete
follow-up avoids missing outcomes for this assessment, as
[the box in Section 5.3](#ch03-justify-equal-variance) records. This
combination of estimates, conditions, and scope makes the result
interpretable [@appelbaum2018].

Suppose the researchers now replace the primary assessment because a
different one gives a larger difference. They have changed the outcome
and selected it after inspection. The report should identify the
original result, the new comparison, the timing and reason for the
change, and the analyses considered. The new result can motivate
further work; its ordinary p-value cannot be presented as if it arose
from the original advance-specified procedure.

## Reading Bridge {#sec-ch03-bridge}

This chapter used a stated repetition to quantify uncertainty about one
estimate. We specified the estimand and the estimator, named the
repetition behind the uncertainty, and calculated standard errors,
pooling two group variances under a common spread. We built confidence
intervals, read their confidence level, and carried out tests from the
same procedure, first for one mean and then for the practice study. The
t tests formed one family, from one sample through paired scores to two
independent groups with equal or unequal spreads, and the same test
logic carried over to the association between two categorical
variables through expected counts and the chi-square distribution,
with a three-way table read as two-way tables within layers. Pairing,
clustering and the school-blocked
design showed that the units which vary independently, not the count of
records, carry the uncertainty. We closed by reading magnitude, the
errors a decision rule can make and the choices made after seeing
results together in one qualified conclusion.

Chapter 4 compares several groups at once. It extends the pooled
variance to several groups as the within-group mean square, splits
variation into between-group and within-group parts, forms the F ratio,
estimates specific contrasts with a calibration for the family of
comparisons, and reads main effects and interaction in a two-factor
design. The SE, interval, testing and selection ideas developed here
will be used at each step.

### Key terms {.unnumbered}

Use this short reference to revisit the main concepts as needed. The
Part One Concept Reference gives the broader reference and the
principal home of each concept, including the sampling ideas developed
in Chapter 2.

```{=latex}
\begingroup\small
```

| Term and common alternatives | Meaning |
|:--|:--|
| Estimate | A numerical approximation to an estimand, calculated from the available data. A point estimate expresses the approximation as one value. |
| Estimator | The rule used to calculate an estimate from data. Its bias and precision concern how the rule behaves across the repetitions specified by the study's procedure or model. |
| Bias (of an estimator) | The difference between an estimator's expected value over the specified repetitions and the estimand. An unbiased estimator has bias zero; precision describes its spread, a separate quality. |
| Pooled variance ($s_p^2$; pooled within-group variance) | A weighted average of within-group sample variances, each weighted by its degrees of freedom: $s_p^2=\{(n_1-1)s_1^2+(n_0-1)s_0^2\}/(n_1+n_0-2)$ for two groups. It estimates a variance the groups are assumed to share; its square root is the pooled SD. |
| Confidence interval (CI) | An interval expressing uncertainty about an estimand. Under its conditions, the procedure covers that estimand at its stated rate across repetitions; the rate describes the procedure. |
| Critical value | The cut-point of a reference distribution, such as the Normal or t, selected by a confidence or significance level. It multiplies the SE in an interval and marks the rejection region of a test. |
| Coverage | The proportion of repetitions in which an interval procedure contains the estimand under its conditions. The confidence level is the procedure's target coverage, not a probability for one realized interval. |
| Null hypothesis | The statistical proposition used as the reference for a test, such as equality of specified population means. The alternative hypothesis states the departure being considered. |
| Test statistic | A quantity calculated from data to assess departure from a null hypothesis. The test compares it with a reference distribution justified under that null and stated conditions. |
| p-value | Under a specified null hypothesis and conditions, the probability of a test result at least as extreme as the observed one, using the test's stated tail rule. |
| Significance level (alpha) | The threshold used for rejecting a null hypothesis, chosen to control the probability of rejecting a true null under the test's conditions. This error is called a Type I error. |
| One-sample z test; one-sample t test | Both compare a sample mean with a stated null mean using its SE; z uses a known process SD under its model, whereas t estimates that SD and uses the appropriate t reference. Neither choice follows an automatic sample-size cutoff. |
| Paired-samples t test | A one-sample t test of within-pair differences against a specified mean difference, with independent pairs under the stated model. |
| Equal-variance two-sample t test (pooled t test; Student's two-sample t test) | One of the two independent-samples t tests. It compares two independent group means under the condition that the populations share one variance: its SE is $s_p\sqrt{1/n_1+1/n_0}$, and its reference is t with $n_1+n_0-2$ df. |
| Welch's unequal-variance t test (Welch test) | The other independent-samples t test. It compares two independent group means without assuming a common variance: its SE adds the two estimated mean variances, and its approximate t reference uses Welch--Satterthwaite df. With equal group sizes its statistic equals the equal-variance statistic, and only the df can differ. |
| Expected count | The count a cell of a two-way table would have under a stated null pattern such as independence, given the observed margins: row total times column total, divided by the overall total. |
| Pearson's chi-square statistic ($X^2$) | The sum over cells of squared differences between observed and expected counts, each divided by its expected count, compared with a chi-square reference with $(R-1)(C-1)$ degrees of freedom under the stated model. |
| Multiway table (three-way table; layered two-way tables) | A table that cross-classifies three or more categorical variables: a two-way table holds two variables, a three-way table three, and a four-way table four. A three-way table is read as two-way tables within the layers of the third variable; a chi-square test of one two-way table cannot test the variables jointly, which needs a method that uses all three variables at once, such as a model for multiway tables. |
| Standardized mean difference | A difference in means divided by a specified SD. The chosen denominator determines the standardized quantity; the raw difference retains the outcome's original units. |
| Power (statistical power) | The probability of rejecting the null under a specified alternative, design, and test. Failure to reject under that alternative is a Type II error; power is one minus its probability. |

: Selected concepts for estimates, uncertainty, and tests. {#tbl-ch03-key-terms tbl-colwidths="[28,72]"}

```{=latex}
\endgroup
```

### Further reading {.unnumbered}

The GAISE College Report emphasizes statistical investigation,
conceptual understanding, and interpretation [@asa2016gaise].
*Introduction to Modern Statistics* develops inference through
repetition, with separate treatments of paired means and two-way
tables [@cetinkaya2024]. [Penn State STAT 200, Lesson 4](https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat200/Lesson04)
connects interval construction with its interpretation. The ASA
p-value statement [@wasserstein2016] and [Moving to a World Beyond
$p<.05$](https://doi.org/10.1080/00031305.2019.1583913) explain why
uncertainty and context deserve more attention than a threshold label.

These exercises use the information supplied and a standard calculator. They practise interpretation, the reading of the chapter's figures and tables, and the conditions behind a conclusion, with a short calculation where the reasoning needs it.

A report states:

> The estimand was the mean Special-minus-Usual assignment contrast in

> 3.1 points, with an estimated standard error of 1.1325 points.

Identify:

1. the estimand;
2. the estimator;
3. the estimation process;
4. the estimate and one statistic used in obtaining it;
5. the standard error and what varies in its repeated-process interpretation;
6. the parameter; and

### Exercise 2: Match the SE to the unit of assignment (Foundational) {.unnumbered #ex-ch03-02}

An invented first-year course compared Special and Usual Practice on a common
0--40 assessment taken two weeks after four practice sessions. Its 120
students belonged to six tutorial classes of 20. The course randomly
assigned whole classes, three to each format, so every student
practised in the format given to their class. Each format therefore
has 60 students. The Special and Usual Practice means are 27.1 and
24.0 points, a difference of 3.1 points, and their delayed-score
SDs are 6.0 and 6.4 points. The three Special Practice classes had
means of 29.4, 26.6 and 25.3 points; the three Usual Practice classes
had means of 26.3, 24.2 and 21.5 points.

An analyst proposes this SE for the Special-minus-Usual difference,

$$
\widehat{SE}=\sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1}+\frac{s_0^2}{n_0}},
$$

with $n_1=n_0=60$ students.

1. What changed from assigning students one at a time? Name the
   independent units of assignment, and explain whether the proposed
   SE describes the uncertainty of the Special-minus-Usual difference
   under this design. Does the change affect the estimate, its SE, or
   both?
2. With these inputs the proposed SE is 1.1325 points. How many units
   of assignment does this calculation assume, and what would have to
   be true of the students' scores for it to describe the uncertainty
   under class assignment?
3. Treat each class mean as one observation. The SDs of the three
   class means are 2.0952 points for Special Practice and 2.4062 points
   for Usual Practice. Calculate the SE from the same formula with
   $n_1=n_0=3$ classes and compare it with 1.1325 points. On a t
   reference with 4 df, the 95% interval for the difference is
   $[-2.0145,\ 8.2145]$. Which conclusion about Special Practice
   remains supported?
4. Which quantities describe variation among students' scores, which
   describe variation among class means, and which estimates variation
   of the mean difference across possible assignments of the classes?

### Exercise 4: Translate a p-value (Foundational) {.unnumbered #ex-ch03-04}

For the matching two-sided zero-contrast test, *t*(118) = 2.7372 and
*p* = .0072. Consider four interpretations:

A. There is a 0.72% probability that the null hypothesis is true.

B. There is a 99.28% probability that Special Practice will work again.

C. Under the zero-contrast null model and the stated procedure, results at
least as incompatible as the observed one have probability about .0072.

D. The 3.1-point effect is educationally important because *p* = .0072.

Choose the defensible interpretation and diagnose each rejected one.
Then:

1. Section 4.4 re-assigns the 120 students' scores at random to two
   groups of 60, 10,000 times, supposing that no student's score
   depends on format; 77 re-assignments give a difference at least 3.1
   points from zero.
   State what the re-assignments held fixed and what they re-drew,
   and what the share 77/10,000 = .0077 estimates.
2. Explain why .0077 is close to, but need not equal, the t test's
   *p* = .0072.
3. The 95% interval from the same procedure as the t test is
   [0.8572, 5.3428]. Explain why its exclusion of zero agrees with
   the two-sided *p* < .05 result, without implying exact
   randomization calibration.
4. Write one sentence reporting estimate, interval, and p-value
   without using **prove**, **accept**, or **worked**.

No calculation is needed; the tail areas and the interval are
supplied.

State what information should be reported about the original and new analyses,

## Appendix A: Probability and Repetition Foundations {.unnumbered #app-probability}

This appendix derives two results behind the chapter's uncertainty
calculations, each for its stated repetition: drawing observations from
a model, or reassigning the same participants.

### Variance, sample variance, and least squares {.unnumbered #app-ch03-variance}

The variance of a random variable is its expected squared distance from
its expectation: $\operatorname{Var}(Y)=E\{(Y-E(Y))^2\}$. For fixed
weights $a_i$ and observations with finite second moments,

$$
\operatorname{Var}\left(\sum_i a_iY_i\right)
=\sum_i a_i^2\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)
+2\sum_{i<j}a_ia_j\operatorname{Cov}(Y_i,Y_j).
$$

Here covariance is the expected product of two centered observations,
and $i<j$ includes each distinct pair once. Expanding the square of the
weighted sum gives the squared terms and the cross-products in this
identity. For an average, every weight is $1/n$; independent
observations have zero covariance, so with common variance $\sigma^2$
the expression becomes $n\sigma^2/n^2=\sigma^2/n$. For a difference,
weights $1$ and $-1$ instead give
$\operatorname{Var}(U)+\operatorname{Var}(V)-2\operatorname{Cov}(U,V)$.
These two applications explain the mean, independent-group, and
paired-difference calculations, and the covariance terms are those
Section 2.3 uses for pairing, clustering and the design effect.

Estimating $\sigma^2$ uses the sample variance
$s^2=\sum_i(Y_i-\bar Y)^2/(n-1)$. For independent observations with
common mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$,

$$
\sum_i(Y_i-\bar Y)^2=\sum_i(Y_i-\mu)^2-n(\bar Y-\mu)^2 .
$$

The first term on the right has expectation $n\sigma^2$ and the second
$n(\sigma^2/n)=\sigma^2$, so $E(s^2)=(n\sigma^2-\sigma^2)/(n-1)=\sigma^2$.
For the values 2, 4 and 6 the mean is 4 and the squared deviations sum
to 8, so $s^2=8/2=4.0000$, whereas dividing by 3 gives 2.6667.
Normality is unnecessary for this result, and an unbiased $s^2$ does not
make $s$ unbiased for $\sigma$. The same algebra with observed values
and any proposed center $a$ gives

$$
\sum_i(y_i-a)^2=\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2+n(\bar y-a)^2 ,
$$

whose last term is nonnegative and vanishes at $a=\bar y$: the mean
minimizes the sum of squared deviations, the **least-squares** property
Chapter 2 states.

### Random assignment and the familiar SE {.unnumbered #app-ch03-assignment}

For the fixed $N=120$ Special Practice participants, let $S_1^2$ and
$S_0^2$ be the potential-outcome variances under the two assignments,
with divisor $N-1$. Let $S_{\mathrm{eff}}^2$ be the variance of the
individual effects $Y_{i1}-Y_{i0}$, using the same divisor. Under
complete random assignment of $n_1$ and $n_0$ participants, consistent
conditions and no relevant interference [@bai2024],

$$
\operatorname{Var}_{\mathrm{assign}}(\bar Y_1-\bar Y_0)
=\frac{S_1^2}{n_1}+\frac{S_0^2}{n_0}-\frac{S_{\mathrm{eff}}^2}{N},
\qquad
E_{\mathrm{assign}}\left(\frac{s_1^2}{n_1}+\frac{s_0^2}{n_0}\right)
=\operatorname{Var}_{\mathrm{assign}}(\bar Y_1-\bar Y_0)+\frac{S_{\mathrm{eff}}^2}{N}.
$$

Only one potential outcome is observed per participant, so the
individual-effect variance is unidentified. The familiar summed
variance is therefore conservative in expectation under this
complete-assignment design, with equality when individual effects are
constant; with equal group sizes it equals the pooled squared SE of
Section 2.2. A particular estimate need not be too large, and the
property does not by itself make the equal-variance or Welch t reference
exact or ensure conservative finite-sample coverage.

A zero average effect allows positive and negative individual effects
to cancel, whereas the stronger **sharp null** says that every
participant's effect is zero. The re-assignments of Section 4.4 test
that sharp null by reproducing the actual assignment mechanism, so
their reference owes nothing to a Normal or t model.

## Appendix B: Inferential Extensions {.unnumbered #app-procedures}

This appendix gathers two references for the chapter's procedures: a
table of their conditions and the steps of a bootstrap, which the
checks of the procedures call on.

@tbl-ch03-procedures collects the five procedures of Sections 5 and 6
with the conditions each relies on, the evidence that checks them and the
response when a condition fails. Each procedure's choices and defaults
stay with its *Justifying the analysis* box, because they vary with the
study rather than the procedure.

|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| One-sample t test: the mean $\mu$ of the sampled population, in outcome units, compared with a stated null value | Random sampling from the named population; independent units, each measured once | A Normal population gives an exact t reference; otherwise the sample mean needs a near-Normal sampling distribution. Look for strong skew, heavy tails or one dominating value in the scores; no sample-size cutoff settles the question | Dependent units: an SE that represents the pairs or clusters (Ch. 3, Sec. 2.3). Strong skew with few units: disclose the weaker approximation and compare a bootstrap interval (Ch. 3, App. B). Without random sampling, a population reading needs a stated model | Ch. 3, Sec. 5.1 |
| Paired-samples t test: the mean within-pair difference $\mu_D$, in outcome units, with the subtraction direction stated | Pairs formed by the design, such as one student measured twice or two classes in one school; independent pairs. Random assignment within pairs supports a causal reading | Near-Normal pair differences give the t reference: inspect the differences themselves rather than the two sets of scores; a few pairs say little about shape | Ignoring the pairing: an independent-groups analysis omits the within-pair covariance and misstates the SE (Ch. 3, Sec. 5.2). No untreated comparison: a mean change alone cannot be separated from time trends or repeated testing. Skewed differences: resample whole pairs (Ch. 3, App. B) | Ch. 3, Sec. 5.2 |
| Equal-variance two-sample t test: a difference between two means, in outcome units, either a mean assignment effect over the participants or a difference between two populations' means | Random assignment of individuals, supporting a causal comparison among the participants, or two independent random samples; different units in the two groups | One common population variance and a near-Normal sampling distribution of the difference: compare the group SDs with the group sizes and look for skew or dominating values in each group. After random assignment the t reference is approximate. ### Resampling and uncertainty {.unnumbered #app-ch03-resampling}

A **bootstrap distribution** approximates an estimator's variability by
repeatedly resampling from observed data. Its center is usually near the
observed estimate. In a simple case bootstrap for independent observations:

1. Identify the independent observational unit and the original number of units.
2. Draw that many units with replacement from the observed units.
3. Apply the same estimator to the resampled data.
4. Repeat the resampling and estimation many times.
5. Use the distribution of estimates to examine variability or construct an appropriate interval.

The bootstrap SE is the sample SD of the resulting estimates. It is
distinct from the SD of individual observations and from the uncertainty
caused by using only finitely many simulation repetitions. Preserve the
study structure: resample pairs together, or clusters when independent
clusters are the appropriate units. Resampling individual students from
clustered classes can misrepresent uncertainty, and the number
resampled is the observed unit count. As Section 4.4 explains, a
bootstrap distribution centered near the estimate is not a reference
for testing zero, and resampling cannot recover unobserved cases or
repair biased selection, invalid measurement, or an unsuitable estimand.
